section_summary: This section centers on the Japan News-Week’s presentation of American views in Japan, including editorials urging clearer Japanese diplomacy, criticizing the Tripartite Pact and Nazi expansion, and defending American aid to Britain. Embassy and Department of State correspondence also examines the newspaper’s financial difficulties, Japanese censorship and pressure on advertisers, and a proposal for support through American motion-picture advertising. The closing documents monitor Japanese press opinion on U.S. policy, the China conflict, the European war, and Japanese-American relations.

subfiles.title: “Japan’s Obligation”
subfiles.about: An editorial calls upon Ambassador Nomura and the Japanese government to explain Japan’s aims clearly to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Editorial "Japan's Obligation" welcomes Nomura's cordial American reception as a sign of hope for peace, argues Japan's New Order and Greater East Asia program stay vague, and says talks need Japan to state what it wants, what others concede and what it offers.

subfiles.title: “Sales Talk”
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper editorial enclosure with duplicated pages
subfiles.about: An editorial rejects Japanese attempts to portray the Tripartite Pact as harmless to American interests and supportive of peace and racial equality.
subfiles.summary: Editorial "Sales Talk": Americans see the Germany-Italy pact as a threat to deter aid to Britain, it criticizes defenses of German conquest and Matsuoka's racial-equality claim, and warns repeated peaceful-alliance sales talk deepens distrust; pages 45-48 duplicate scans.

subfiles.title: Letter from Joseph C. Grew to W. R. Wills
subfiles.about: Grew urges Wills not to criticize Roosevelt and Hull for distinguishing the Axis threat from Soviet Russia.
subfiles.summary: Grew tells W. R. Wills the Axis posed an avowed threat to the U.S. unlike Soviet Russia then, warns that an editorial attacking the President and Secretary of State would draw serious criticism, and says Americans abroad should support or at least not openly censure government policy.

subfiles.title: Follow-up memorandum on advertising support for Japan News-Week
subfiles.about: An internal memorandum records the status of efforts to obtain motion-picture-industry advertising for the Japan News-Week.
subfiles.summary: Memo: the Embassy hadn't answered the Department's suggestion that American film representatives in Japan recommend ad support for Japan News-Week to Mr. Hays; the division hadn't yet spoken to Carl Milliken but intended to.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on financing Japan News-Week through motion-picture advertising
subfiles.about: The Far Eastern Affairs division evaluates a proposal for American motion-picture companies to advertise in and thereby support the Japan News-Week.
subfiles.summary: Memo reviews Japan News-Week's lost Japanese advertising and Grew's belief it usefully presents the American view; it doubts the paper's earlier pro-Japanese reputation, warns conspicuous backing might get it suppressed, and recommends consulting film representatives and briefing Carl Milliken.

subfiles.title: Telegram 418 concerning Japan News-Week
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports pressure on the Japan News-Week, its financial difficulties, and a proposal for institutional advertising by American motion-picture companies.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 418: Wills rejected selling to the Japan Information Bureau, Mitsui and Mitsubishi pulled ads under apparent pressure, he declined a direct British subsidy, and Grew endorses the paper and asks State to approach Will Hays about a campaign of about 500 yen monthly.

subfiles.title: Telegram 204 on Japan News-Week advertising
subfiles.about: The Department authorizes preliminary consultation with American motion-picture representatives concerning advertising support for the Japan News-Week.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 204: State is considering an informal approach to Mr. Hays on Tokyo's telegram 418; meanwhile the Embassy may tell company representatives State will pass their recommendation to Hays.

subfiles.title: Opening page of memorandum on despatch 5500
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes two Japan News-Week editorials forwarded with Embassy despatch 5500.
subfiles.summary: Memo on despatch 5500: an editorial contrasts Roosevelt's March 15 speech with Hitler's, saying American aid opposes forcible conquest rather than any domestic government form and so needn't preclude cooperation with Japan.

subfiles.title: Detached duplicate page from “Grim Contrast”
subfiles.about: A detached duplicate concluding page of “Grim Contrast” explains the principles behind American foreign assistance.
subfiles.summary: Detached page from "Grim Contrast": America doesn't condition aid on democratic form but opposes powers imposing systems by force, and friendship with Japan remains possible if it avoids conquest and negotiates peacefully with Indochina, Thailand and the Indies.

subfiles.title: Continuation of May 1 memorandum on despatch 5500
subfiles.about: The continuation summarizes the Japan News-Week editorial “Autonomous Japan.”
subfiles.summary: May 1 memo on despatch 5500: the editorial answers a Japanese reader saying attacking one Tripartite power means attacking all, warning that surrendering autonomy to a Nazi-dominated superstate would destroy Japan's unifying institutions.

subfiles.title: Despatch 5500: Editorials on Roosevelt’s speech and the Tripartite Alliance
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits and analyzes two Japan News-Week editorials presenting American views on the war and Japan’s relationship with the Axis.
subfiles.summary: The despatch summarizes “Grim Contrast,” which contrasts Roosevelt’s defense of freedom and small nations with Hitler’s racial doctrines, conquest, and uncertain predictions of British defeat. It then analyzes “Autonomous Japan,” which rejects the idea that the Tripartite Pact makes Japan, Germany, and Italy a single entity and warns against sacrificing Japan’s national polity to Nazi totalitarianism. Grew submits the pieces as examples of vigorous pro-American commentary surviving Japanese censorship.

subfiles.title: “Grim Contrast”
subfiles.about: The editorial contrasts Roosevelt’s democratic and humanitarian program with Hitler’s vision of conquest and racial domination.
subfiles.summary: "Grim Contrast": Roosevelt's speech rejects appeasement and defends freedom and dignity; Hitler's justifies conquest, racial superiority and destroying small states, his shifting timetable for Britain's collapse showing uncertainty; American aid targets forcible domination, not any domestic government.

subfiles.title: “Autonomous Japan”
subfiles.about: The editorial answers a Japanese reader who objected to criticism of Germany and argues that Japan must retain its autonomy within the Tripartite Alliance.
subfiles.summary: "Autonomous Japan": American aid to Chongqing, Greece and Britain rests on strategic and moral grounds, not claimed democracy; criticizing Germany doesn't attack Japan since the alliance doesn't merge them; Nazi-style totalitarianism would sacrifice Japan's imperial polity and sovereignty.

subfiles.title: Telegram on official censure and financial support for Japan News-Week
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports official criticism of the Japan News-Week and the subsequent restoration of Japanese advertising.
subfiles.summary: Wills told Grew the Information Bureau censured him for anti-German material, which he answered with his pro-friendship policy; the Bureau and Navy wanted the paper to continue and offered a 10,000-yen subsidy, which he refused; after he sought commercial ads, Mitsui restored its contract and Mitsubishi was expected to.

subfiles.title: Telegram 627: Japanese press reaction and diplomatic themes
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy summarizes Japanese press discussion of American policy, Matsuoka, aid to Chongqing, and the European war.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 627: vernacular papers belittled expanded American patrols, stressed American divisions and sympathized with Lindbergh; Kokumin argued the Axis tie aims to keep America out and Japan should end aid to Chiang; another editorial urged Germany to defeat Britain first.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Unfavorable cartoon of President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to another file containing an unfavorable Roosevelt cartoon and a conversation with editor Toshi Go.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's despatch 5469 with copies of an unfavorable Roosevelt cartoon in the Japan Times and Advertiser and a conversation memo with editor Toshi Go.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on despatch 5575 and “No Compromise”
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes the Japan News-Week editorial “No Compromise” and comments on the departure of its associate editor.
subfiles.summary: Memo on despatch 5575: "No Compromise" rebuts Japanese claims aid to Britain is futile from German strength, isolationists and labor unrest, insisting American policy rests on principles and would continue even if Britain fell; associate editor C. N. Spinks left but the paper's policy will continue.

subfiles.title: Despatch 5575: Transmitting “No Compromise”
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits and analyzes a Japan News-Week editorial defending American aid to Britain and predicting possible intervention in the war.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 5575: a Japanese reader doubted aid to Britain given shipping, German power, isolationists and labor disputes; "No Compromise" calls American policy an immutable commitment to destroying Nazi-Fascist power, possibly by intervention; it was departing associate editor C. N. Spinks's last editorial in the series.

subfiles.title: “No Compromise”
subfiles.about: The editorial argues that military reverses, isolationism, and labor disputes will not deter the United States from defeating Nazi-Fascism.
subfiles.summary: "No Compromise": after Axis victories in Yugoslavia, Greece and North Africa, American aid to Britain serves ideals beyond British victory; Lindbergh doesn't represent national opinion, American labor disputes concern wages and hours, and policy is immutable, with intervention possible if aid fails.

subfiles.title: “Desires Enlightenment”
subfiles.about: A reader questions whether American assistance can save Britain and whether defense-industry labor unrest will undermine U.S. policy.
subfiles.summary: A reader's letter praises German preparedness, says shipping shortages, submarines and landing difficulties make aid to Britain hopeless, and, citing Lindbergh, asks whether Roosevelt could constitutionally suppress defense strikes or labor leaders were obstructing aid.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for Mr. Berle transmitting a newspaper report
subfiles.about: A brief memorandum forwards a report comparing the attitudes of two Japanese-American newspapers.
subfiles.summary: Memo to Berle submits a comparison of Japanese-American newspaper attitudes for the Far Eastern and Intelligence Divisions.

subfiles.title: Report comparing Japanese-American newspapers
subfiles.about: The report compares English- and Japanese-language Japanese-American newspaper content from May 17 and May 31, 1941.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese American Review calls American aid to Chiang imperialistic, defends Wang Ching-wei and praises the November 1940 treaty; the Japanese American criticizes frozen balances, praises Roosevelt and predicts U.S. entry without a declaration; the May 31 discussion compares Japan's terms with the Treaty of Tianjin and Boxer Protocol.
